title: Apollo 11 Lunar Module — Descent Stage "Eagle"
what: The lower half of the lander. It carried the descent engine, fuel, landing gear and the science packages down to the surface.
why: It was never meant to come home. The descent stage stayed behind as the launch platform for the ascent stage that carried Armstrong and Aldrin back to orbit.
science: Its landing proved a crewed vehicle could touch down and lift off from another world. It is still standing at Tranquility Base.

title: Passive Seismic Experiment (EASEP)
what: A solar-powered seismometer, levelled by hand on the regolith and shielded from the Sun.
why: To listen for moonquakes and meteorite strikes, and use them to read the Moon’s interior.
science: It found the Moon rings for a long time after an impact — evidence of a dry, fractured crust. It ran for three weeks before overheating.

title: Laser Ranging Retroreflector (LRRR)
what: An array of corner-cube prisms that sends incoming laser light back toward its source.
why: So observatories on Earth could fire a laser at the Moon and time how long light takes to return.
science: Still in use today. It showed the Moon is drifting away from Earth by about 3.8 centimetres a year — the only Apollo experiment still returning data.

title: Surveyor 3
what: A three-legged robotic lander with a scoop on an arm, sent before anyone knew whether a spacecraft would sink into the lunar surface.
why: To prove a soft landing was possible, and to find out whether the ground could hold a crewed lander. Its engine cut out late, so it bounced twice before settling.
science: It showed the regolith was firm enough to land on and walk on. Two and a half years later Apollo 12 touched down about 180 m away — the only time anyone has gone back to visit something we had left behind. Conrad and Bean cut pieces off it and carried them home; its TV camera is in the Smithsonian.

title: Apollo 12 ALSEP
what: The first full Apollo science station: a central transmitter, a seismometer, and a SNAP-27 nuclear generator standing off to one side on its own cable.
why: Apollo 11's seismometer ran on sunlight and died within weeks. This one had a radioisotope generator, so it could keep working through the two-week lunar night.
science: Days after the crew left, their ascent stage was deliberately crashed into the Moon 73 km away. This seismometer heard the Moon ring for about 55 minutes — dry, deeply fractured rock with no water in it to damp the shaking. It kept listening until every ALSEP station was switched off on 30 September 1977.

title: Apollo 15 Lunar Module — Descent Stage "Falcon"
what: The lower half of the lander: engine, tanks, landing gear, and the bays that carried the rover and the science packages down.
why: Like Eagle at Tranquility, it was the launch platform the ascent stage pushed off from. It was never coming back.
science: Apollo 15 was the first of the long stays — three days on the surface and nearly 19 hours outside, against Apollo 11's two and a half. It still stands here, and orbiting cameras still use it as a fixed point.

title: Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV-1)
what: A folding, battery-electric car that rode down strapped to the side of the lander. Four wheels of woven piano wire, a top speed of about 13 km/h, and two antennas: a low-gain antenna oriented during traverses and a high-gain dish for television when stopped.
why: To get the crew out to the mountain front and the edge of Hadley Rille and back, carrying tools and rock boxes, within walking distance of safety if it ever failed.
science: It turned a landing site into a field area: Apollo 15 covered about 28 km of ground in three drives. The dish is the reason anyone on Earth saw it happen — but it had to be stopped and re-aimed at Earth before the pictures could come.

title: Laser Ranging Retroreflector (Apollo 15)
what: Three hundred corner-cube prisms in two panels — three times the array Apollo 11 left, and still the largest on the Moon.
why: More cubes means more photons come home, so observatories can range on it in worse conditions and get a cleaner measurement.
science: You have seen one of these before, at Tranquility. With 300 corner cubes, this is the largest Apollo reflector array; Apollo 11 and 14 each left 100. The arrays remain part of lunar laser-ranging research, the Apollo surface experiment still returning data more than fifty years on.

title: Opportunity (MER-B)
what: A solar-powered field geologist the size of a golf cart: six wheels, a camera mast at about eye height, and an arm carrying a microscope and a rock grinder.
why: To find out whether Mars ever had liquid water on its surface, by reading the rocks directly instead of guessing from orbit.
science: In its first weeks, it found layered rocks and hematite spherules that supported a watery past. Built for 90 sols, Opportunity worked for more than 5,000 and drove 45.16 km. It held the off-Earth driving-distance record until Perseverance passed it on 11 October 2026, reaching 45.22 km.

title: Opportunity's Heat Shield
what: The shield that took the heat of entry, thrown away a few kilometres up and left where it hit. It struck hard enough to turn itself inside out.
why: It was never meant to be visited. It is here because something had to be discarded for the rover to arrive at all.
science: Opportunity drove back to photograph its own discarded shield — and found an iron meteorite lying beside it, the first meteorite ever identified on another planet. It was named Heat Shield Rock.

title: Mars Pathfinder — Carl Sagan Memorial Station
what: A lander that arrived wrapped in airbags, bounced across the plain at least fifteen times — the first rebounds about fifteen metres high — then rolled to a stop and opened three petals like a flower.
why: To prove a cheap, fast way of landing on Mars: no retro-rockets all the way down, just a parachute, an airbag cocoon, and a bounce. And to deliver the first rover.
science: It sent back the first colour panoramas of an Ares Vallis flood plain and measured the weather for 83 sols. The airbag method it proved was used again to put Spirit and Opportunity on Mars. It was renamed the Carl Sagan Memorial Station after it landed.

title: Sojourner
what: A rover the size of a microwave oven: 10.6 kg, six wheels on a rocker-bogie suspension, one solar panel, and a spectrometer it pressed against rocks to read their chemistry.
why: To prove that a wheeled robot could be driven on another planet at all. Nobody had done it before.
science: It drove about 100 metres in 83 sols and never went more than a few metres from the lander — but it measured the rocks around it and showed they were varied, which meant Ares Vallis really was a flood plain. Its rocker-bogie suspension is still the design every Mars rover uses, Perseverance included.

title: Viking 1 Lander
what: A three-legged lander the size of a small car, powered by two plutonium generators rather than sunlight, with a scoop on an arm and a weather mast.
why: To take the first pictures from the surface of Mars, and to run the first experiments looking for life in the soil.
science: It returned the first clear photographs ever taken from the Martian surface, and worked for more than six years — far beyond its 90-day design. Its biology experiments gave results nobody could agree on, which is part of why we are still sending landers.

title: Viking 2 Lander
what: Viking 1's identical twin, set down on the other side of the planet.
why: Two landers in two very different places, so the results could be compared rather than guessed at. That is how you tell a local oddity from something true of the whole planet.
science: It photographed thin water frost forming on the ground in winter — the first time anyone saw weather happen on another planet's surface. Its batteries failed after three and a half years.

title: Spirit (MER-A)
what: Opportunity's identical twin, landed on the other side of Mars three weeks earlier.
why: Gusev Crater has a dry river valley running into it, so it looked like a crater lake that had drained. The idea was to read the bottom of it.
science: It found what it was sent for in the hills above the crater floor: rocks altered by water, and almost pure silica of the kind that forms around hot springs. In 2009 it broke through a crust into soft sand and could not get out, and with one wheel already dead it could not be angled toward the winter Sun. It kept working where it stood until the cold took it.

title: Phoenix Mars Lander
what: A solar-powered lander with a digging arm, set down far enough north to reach ice a few centimetres below the surface.
why: To touch Martian water directly instead of inferring it from orbit, and to find out whether the soil could support life.
science: It dug down, found bright material, and watched it vanish over a few days — ice turning straight to vapour. Then it melted ice in an onboard oven and confirmed it was water. The icy soil was so sticky it clung inside the upside-down scoop and the team had to shake it loose. When the arctic winter came the sunlight ran out, exactly as planned.

title: InSight
what: A lander that never moved: two wide solar wings, and a seismometer it lifted off its own deck and set down on the ground under a wind shield.
why: To listen to the inside of Mars. A seismometer reads a planet's interior the way the Apollo instruments read the Moon's.
science: It recorded well over a thousand marsquakes and used them to measure the crust, mantle and core — the first time anyone has sounded the inside of another planet. Dust built up on its panels year after year until there was not enough power left to answer. The site was deliberately chosen to be boring: flat, safe and quiet, because the science was underground.

title: Ingenuity
year: First flight 19 April 2021 · last flight 18 January 2024
what: A helicopter weighing under two kilograms, with two rotors turning in opposite directions at over 2,000 rpm because the air here is about one percent as thick as Earth's.
why: To find out whether powered flight on another planet was possible at all. It carried no science instruments: it was there to prove the idea.
science: Its first hop lasted 39 seconds and was the first powered, controlled flight anywhere but Earth. It was meant to fly five times. It flew 72, scouting routes for Perseverance, until a rotor blade was damaged on landing and it could not fly safely again. It is still standing where it came down.

title: Ranger 4
what: A early lunar probe carrying cameras and a balsa-wood capsule with a seismometer inside, meant to survive a rough landing. Its onboard computer failed hours after launch, so the solar panels never opened and nothing ever switched on.
why: To get the first close-up pictures of the Moon, and to put the first seismometer on another world — seven years before Apollo 11 managed it.
science: It returned no data at all. It drifted, dead, until the Moon got in the way, and hit the far side at about 9,600 km/h. It was still the first US spacecraft to reach another celestial body, and the first object of any nation to reach the far-side surface. Everything else you have found out here worked first. This one never did — and we came anyway.

title: NEAR Shoemaker
what: A spacecraft built to orbit an asteroid, not to land on one. It has no landing legs: four solar panels, a dish antenna, and a camera on the end of a body the size of a small car.
why: To spend a year circling Eros, mapping it up close — the first spacecraft ever to orbit an asteroid.
science: When the year was up, the team brought it down anyway, though it was never designed to land. It came down at about walking pace, survived, and kept transmitting from the surface for more than two weeks — the first spacecraft ever to land on an asteroid. It is still lying here, just south of the saddle-shaped valley called Himeros.
